title: Why So Many Languages?
objective: After this level you can explain why languages like Python, JavaScript and C all exist, each suited to different jobs.
summary: C was built to write Unix and stays close to the machine; JavaScript runs in every major browser; Python is quick to write but, being interpreted, generally slower. Each language is a trade-off.

cards.headline: Why isn't there just one programming language?
cards.body: Because every language is a bargain. Some make life easier for the programmer; others squeeze the most from the machine; one is simply everywhere you browse. Three famous languages show three different bargains.

cards.headline: C: close to the machine
cards.body: Dennis Ritchie turned an earlier language into C at Bell Labs between 1971 and 1973, to write the Unix operating system; in summer 1973 the Unix kernel was rewritten in it. C's types and operations mirror what real processors do, which made it efficient enough to replace assembly language for building systems. Ritchie's own verdict: "C is quirky, flawed, and an enormous success."

cards.headline: JavaScript: the language of the browser
cards.body: Brendan Eich created JavaScript while working at Netscape, and it arrived in the Netscape Navigator 2.0 browser in September 1995. Today it runs primarily in web browsers, where it changes what's on a page, fetches data from servers and draws graphics. Its great strength is reach: every major browser has a JavaScript engine built in.

cards.headline: Python: quick to write, slower to run
cards.body: Guido van Rossum started Python over the 1989 Christmas holidays and posted it publicly in February 1991. It's a high-level, general-purpose language with a large standard library, and it's interpreted. That's its bargain: interpreted languages typically have a shorter write-and-fix cycle than compiled ones, but their programs generally run more slowly. Picking a language means picking which cost you'd rather pay.
